visual_features.distinctive_marks: black markings around the eyes and face, white chest and belly

description: Thomas's langur (Presbytis thomasi), also known as the North Sumatran leaf monkey or Thomas's leaf monkey, is a primate endemic to northern Sumatra, Indonesia, found only north of Lake Toba and the Alas and Wampu rivers. It inhabits subtropical or tropical dry forests. Like other members of the genus Presbytis, this species has evolved to digest cellulose through microbial fermentation in a specialized foregut. Although primarily folivorous, they also eat fruit (usually unripe with high pH to avoid killing gut microbes), flowers, and occasionally toadstools and snails. They live approximately 20 years in the wild and up to 29 years in captivity. Substantial populations exist in Gunung Leuser National Park, particularly in Ketambe and Bukit Lawang.
population_estimate: Population declined by approximately 30% in the last few decades due to ongoing deforestation of the Leuser and Ulu Massen Ecosystems. No precise census available. Protected under Indonesian Law and CITES Appendix II.
habitat: Subtropical or tropical dry forests of northern Sumatra, Indonesia. Found only north of Lake Toba and the Alas and Wampu rivers. Inhabits Gunung Leuser National Park with substantial populations in Ketambe and Bukit Lawang areas. Prefers forested habitats with access to young leaves, which are their preferred food source.
threats: Deforestation of the Leuser and Ulu Massen Ecosystems
Illegal logging and palm oil plantation expansion
Human-wildlife conflict — enters croplands and is culled by farmers
Illegal pet trade — infants are captured after mothers are killed
Habituation to tourists in Gunung Leuser leading to negative human-wildlife interactions
ecosystem_role: Thomas's langur disperses seeds and pollinates flowers of plants they consume. As folivorous primates with specialized digestive systems, they process tough leaves that other herbivores cannot digest, maintaining the balance of plant communities. They are prey for Sunda clouded leopards, Sumatran tigers, Asian golden cats, and reticulated pythons. They serve as an indicator species for forest health in northern Sumatra.
human_connection: Known as 'reungkah' in Acehnese and 'kedih' in Alas languages. They share habitat with critically endangered Sumatran orangutans, Sumatran elephants, and Sumatran tigers, making the protection of their habitat important for multiple flagship species. They are an important ecotourism attraction in Bukit Lawang. However, habituation to tourists has led to negative consequences, with some individuals becoming dependent on human food.
what_students_can_do: Support sustainable palm oil and forest conservation initiatives
Raise awareness about the importance of Gunung Leuser National Park
Study langur social behavior, communication, and dietary ecology
Advocate against the illegal pet trade of wild primates
Practice and encourage responsible wildlife tourism (no feeding wild animals)
fun_fact: Thomas's langurs have a distinctive crown-like 'mohawk' of white fur with a dark grey stripe running through it — one of the most striking hairstyles in the primate world
They primarily eat unripe fruit with high pH levels to avoid killing the specialized microbes in their stomachs that help digest leaves
They drink from naturally occurring tree holes where rainwater collects, or from small forest pools
Juveniles have creamy white fur that gradually changes to the adult grey coloration as they mature
Although they can live 20 years in the wild, in captivity they may live up to 29 years due to the absence of predators and stress
